activity: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
knowledge_domain: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
fact: Masaccio's Holy Trinity fresco in Florence, painted around 1427, is one of the earliest paintings built on a single vanishing point.
story:
The art room smelled like pencil shavings and the lemon cleaner Mr. Francis used on the tables, and Sara's drawing of Maple Street still looked wrong. She had drawn the street four times since Tuesday, and every time it lay flat on the page like a map instead of running back into the distance. Around her, Beatrice was shading a storefront and Abbygail was complaining that her brick pattern "revolved" around being terrible, which was her way of saying it kept coming out crooked no matter where she started.

"You're rushing the rooflines," Beatrice said, peeking over. "Mine did that too, before."

Before. Sara remembered the gallery trip last fall, the rainy Saturday her mother had driven them into the city at the expense of a whole afternoon, just so Sara could see real paintings. She had stood in front of a big print of a fresco, a church interior with vaulted ceiling and columns, and something about it had bothered her until she raised her finger and traced along the ceiling beams. They weren't parallel on the page. They leaned toward each other, and when she followed them with her fingertip, every line she tried, the edges of the floor, the arch, all of them, ran toward one spot near the base of the cross. Beatrice had yanked her hand down before the guard noticed, but Sara had already seen it.

She flipped to a fresh page now and sketched the street fast, one line down the middle for the road. Then she picked a point with her pencil, halfway up the page, dead center, and drew every curb, every roofline, every fence rail slanting toward it. The buildings on the left leaned right; the ones on the right leaned left. It looked strange for a minute, almost impoverished of detail compared with her careful earlier versions, nothing but converging lines and a dot.

Then she added windows, each one smaller as it neared the dot, and stepped back from the desk. The street ran. It actually ran, back and back, until the road narrowed to almost nothing.

"Where'd you learn that?" Beatrice said, leaning across the aisle.

"That fresco, the one in Florence. From the gallery." Sara pulled the print catalogue from her bag, the one she'd spent her allowance on, and found the page. "Masaccio's Holy Trinity. It says it was painted around 1427, and it's one of the earliest paintings built on a single vanishing point." She tapped the caption, then tapped her own dot. "That's what this is. Everything aims there."

Mr. Francis paused behind them on his rounds. "Sara, that's the strongest street in the room," he said, and moved on.

Abbygail slid her chair over and held her crooked brick drawing beside Sara's. "So my vanishing point is wherever my wobbliest lines happen to meet."

"That's one theory," Sara said, and drew a small, careful dot in the corner of Abbygail's page.

activity: to paint a portrait in watercolour by layering washes from light to dark
knowledge_domain: to paint a portrait in watercolour by layering washes from light to dark
fact: Watercolour paint is pigment bound with gum arabic, which lets it dissolve again in water even after it has dried.
story:
Hudson sat at his grandmother's kitchen table with a jar of water, three brushes, and a photograph of Grandpa taken before his fall. That was the whole trouble, actually. Last winter Grandpa had slipped on the porch steps and gotten a concussion, and for weeks he hadn't been allowed to do much but sit in the big chair by the window. He'd watched Hudson draw then, calling out suggestions while Hudson worked, and somehow that was how they'd gotten close again after two years of only seeing each other at holidays. Now Hudson wanted to give him a portrait, painted properly in watercolour, the way Grandma had shown him: light washes first, darker layers on top, each one given time to dry.

The portrait was for Grandpa's birthday, which was Saturday. Today was Thursday, and Hudson had just made a disaster. A dark wash of brown had bled across Grandpa's forehead, making him look like he'd been in a fight. Hudson groaned and, without thinking much, brushed clean water over the spot to soften it. The brown moved. It actually moved, swirling up out of the paper and into his brush like the paint had never dried at all.

"Grandma, come look at this." He dabbed at the spot with a paper towel and the brown came away, leaving the forehead pale again, only a faint shadow left behind.

She leaned over his shoulder, reading her glasses up from her neck. "That's the gum arabic," she said. "It binds the pigment, and it lets the paint dissolve again in water even after it dries." Then she straightened up and went back to her tomatoes on the counter, leaving him to figure out the rest.

Hudson tested the idea before trusting it. On a scrap of paper he painted a dark stripe, let it dry until the shine vanished, then touched it with a wet brush. The stripe bloomed back to life and lifted when he pressed a towel to it. So that was the hidden rule of this paint. Dried did not mean finished. He worked backward through his portrait, wetting the places where he'd gone too dark and lifting them out, then letting the paper dry completely before layering fresh colour. The second portrait was better than the first, and the third better still. Grandpa's face came up out of the paper in slow stages, lighter shapes underneath, shadow settling into the creases around his eyes.

On Saturday, Adeline and Callum came over for cake. When Hudson handed Grandpa the wrapped painting, Callum leaned in and squinted at it. "You made him look kind, Hudson."

"I was biased," Hudson admitted. "I only used the photo from after he got better."

Grandpa peeled back the paper and went quiet, holding the portrait at arm's length the way he held the newspaper. "Well," he said at last. "Tomorrow we paint one of you."

activity: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
knowledge_domain: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
fact: Carbon has atomic number 6, so every carbon atom has six protons in its nucleus.
story:
The periodic table on the museum wall was taller than Ms. Bekele, and Luke stood in front of it with his worksheet flapping in his hand. At the top of the page, in block letters, it said ELEMENT HUNT: FIND THE ELEMENT THAT MAKES UP YOUR PENCIL. First team to answer all ten questions wins a free pass to the simulator room, the exhibit where a giant screen let you simulate a trip through the solar system. Keagan had won the last two class competitions, and Luke still felt a curl of resentment about the second one, which Keagan had won by half a point.

"Pencil," said Makenzie, digging through her backpack. "My mom labels everything." She held up a sharpened pencil with a strip of tape on it that read GRAPHITE, in her mother's careful printing. "So we need graphite, but graphite isn't on the table anywhere."

"Then it's made of something," Luke said. He ran his finger along the rows of colored squares. They went to the minerals case first, where a placard about a crystal display said graphite was a form of carbon. Back at the wall, Luke found CARBON in the sixth square from the top of the second row. Inside the square was a big letter C, the word carbon, and a small 6 at the very top.

"That little number is the atomic number," Makenzie said, reading the legend at the bottom of the display. "It says here the atomic number tells you the number of protons."

"So carbon has atomic number six," Luke said slowly, "which means every carbon atom has six protons in it." He wrote it down, then stopped. Something about it felt strange. Nobody could see a proton. The pencil in Makenzie's hand looked like just gray stuff, and the wall was just paint and metal, but the number was saying something invisible was in there, exactly six of it, every single time. He didn't want to write down something he only half trusted.

"Test it," Makenzie said, chewing the end of her braid. She pointed at the next question on the worksheet, which asked about the oxygen in the air they were breathing. Luke found OXYGEN, read the small 8 at the top of its square, and wrote eight protons. Then he found gold, seventy-nine, and iron, twenty-six. Every square had the number in the same spot, doing the same job. The pattern held all the way down the wall, and the tight feeling in his chest loosened. It wasn't a guess. It was a rule, and the rule worked everywhere he checked.

Across the room, Keagan was staring at his own worksheet with a predatory grin aimed at the scoreboard, which already showed his team ahead by one. Luke wrote the last answer, sprinted to Ms. Bekele by the neon jellyfish tank, and slapped the page onto her clipboard. She checked it, looked up, and said, "All correct. Free passes for the simulator room."

"Half each," Luke told Keagan, holding up two passes. Keagan looked at the passes, then at the wall of elements, and said, "Deal. But next time I'm picking the pencil question."

activity: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
knowledge_domain: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
fact: Stress can also show up in behaviour, such as snapping at friends, having trouble concentrating or losing interest in hobbies, and noticing these signs is the first step to managing it.
story:
Simon had been at his grandparent's house for two days, and so far he had yelled at his little cousin for touching his shoes, dropped his fork at breakfast because his hands felt jumpy, and abandoned the model boat he had started building in the shed, the one he had been excited about all month. His cousin had run off crying, and Simon had stared after him, baffled. He hadn't even cared about the shoes.

On Thursday afternoon he sat on the back step with his grandmother's dog and tried to figure it out, because it felt like something invisible was making everything go wrong. He didn't have a fever. He wasn't coming down with a virus, the way his cousin had last month. Nothing hurt. He made a list in his head, the way he did for science class. Yelling over nothing. Fork dropping. Not wanting to build the boat. He looked at the three items and noticed they all pointed the same direction, like arrows aimed at one hidden cause.

Then he found it. Tryouts were on Monday. He had been telling himself he wasn't worried about them, but every night he had lain awake past eleven, listening to the grandfather clock tick, and every morning he had woken up tired and heavy. It was almost bizarre how obvious it looked once he saw it. He tested the idea out loud. "I'm stressed," he said to the dog. "That's what this is." The signs had been there all week, and he had walked right past them.

He found his grandfather in the garden, tying up tomato plants. "Grandpa, when you get stressed, what do you do?"

His grandfather wiped his hands on his trousers. "Same as anybody, I suppose. I go for a walk. And I breathe slow, in through the nose, out like I'm cooling soup. Want to try it?"

They stood between the tomato rows and breathed together, in for four counts, out for six, until Simon's shoulders came down from where they had been sitting near his ears. That night he did what his grandmother suggested and left his phone in the kitchen, read for a while, and was asleep before the clock struck ten.

Friday he found his cousin in the shed, hovering over the half-built boat. "Sorry I yelled," Simon said. "It wasn't about the shoes." His cousin nodded and held out the glue. They worked until the light went thin and orange through the window, and when Simon's hands fumbled a spar, he noticed the old jumpiness creeping back, put down the glue, and breathed, in through the nose, out like he was cooling soup.

Monday morning he was on the field before the whistle, boots laced, wide awake. Pierce jogged over from the far side and clapped him on the shoulder. "You look different this week."

"I slept," Simon said, and crouched, ready.

activity: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
knowledge_domain: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
fact: Honey should not be given to babies under 12 months old, because it can contain bacteria spores that grow in an infant's gut and cause a serious illness called infant botulism.
story:
Justin had never babysat before, and the note on the fridge made it clear what he was up against. Feed Mia at six o'clock sharp, the note said. Parents back by nine. Beneath that, underlined twice, were three words: no honey, ever. The baby, Mia, sat in her high chair banging a spoon, and Justin realized he had less than ten minutes to figure out dinner.

He opened a cupboard and took a census of the shelves: rice cereal, small jars of pureed carrots and pears, a box of crackers, and a plastic bear full of honey. Mia's older sister, Nelia, was supposed to be at soccer practice, but she limped in through the back door just then, her ankle wrapped, practice cancelled. She dropped her bag on a chair and watched him spoon carrot puree into a bowl.

"It's bland," Justin said. "She won't eat it plain. I was going to stir in a little honey." He reached for the bear.

Nelia grabbed his wrist. "The note. No honey, ever." She pointed at the fridge, and Justin read the rest of it, smaller letters he had skipped: Babies under 12 months old can't have honey. It can carry bacteria spores that grow in a baby's gut and make her seriously sick. Something called infant botulism.

"That's a real thing?" Justin said. He set the bear back on the shelf and washed his hands, then tried a different idea. It seemed plausible that Mia would accept the cereal if it tasted of fruit, so he mixed the pear puree into the bowl instead, a spoonful at a time, and offered it. Mia turned her head away. Justinpersevered anyway, making airplane noises, scraping the spoon against the rim, tilting it so she could see the pears. On the fourth try she opened her mouth.

"Smart," Nelia said. "Pears worked for her last week too." She sat down across from the high chair and let Mia grab one of her fingers.

Justin checked the clock. Six oh two, and the bowl was already half empty, and Mia was smearing orange mush on her tray with obvious satisfaction. When the phone buzzed with a text from the parents asking how it was going, Justin typed back one line and held it up for Nelia to see before sending: "Fed her pears and cereal. No honey."

"Honey never happened," Nelia said, and Mia banged her spoon like a drum.

activity: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
knowledge_domain: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
fact: Earth's axis points in the same direction in space all year, so for part of the orbit the Northern Hemisphere leans toward the Sun and later leans away.
story:
Maria stood in her grandfather's study, holding his old globe with one finger pressed on Canada. The lamp on the desk was the Sun, that was the whole plan, but every time she walked the globe around the lamp, Canada ended up sideways or upside down. Zach sat on the rug with the cat, watching her third failed lap.

"It's broken," Maria said.

"It's not broken, you're turning it," Zach said. He was always this assertive, certain even when he had no proof, and last summer that certainty had cost them a whole afternoon hunting for a "shortcut" that dumped them behind the hardware store instead of the pool. She had followed him then. She wasn't going to follow him now.

"Watch," Zach said. He took the globe, set it on the shelf, and pushed its stand around the lamp in a slow circle, the north pole tipped toward the window the entire way. Maria noticed the pole was like an arrow, and she remembered her grandfather's compass, which had floated in a bowl of water through a documentary about a tsunami, pointing the same direction no matter how the bowl was carried. She fetched a roll of tape and stuck a strip across the ceiling, straight out from the shelf, like a road sign.

"New rule," she said. "The pole has to point at the tape the whole way around. If it doesn't, you're cheating."

Zach walked the globe again, slower this time, checking the tape at every step. On one side of the lamp, Canada leaned right at the bulb, close and bright. He kept going, pole still aimed at the tape, and when the globe reached the far side of the lamp, Canada leaned away, tilted back into shadow. He stopped there. "Whoa. Look at it now."

Maria leaned in. Their side of the world had swung toward the Sun, then away, all without the pole ever moving. She thought of herself in September, insisting to Mr. Ndlovu that seasons came from Earth being closer to the Sun, and how he had only raised an eyebrow and said, "Then why is it autumn in Australia?" She'd walked out annoyed. Now she wanted to march back and take it back.

"Get the flashlight," she said. "We're going to verify the Southern Hemisphere next. Australia gets the opposite."

Zach was already reaching for the drawer.

activity: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
knowledge_domain: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
fact: The first transcontinental railroad in the United States was completed on 10 May 1869 at Promontory Summit, Utah, making the trip west far faster than by wagon.
story:
Isla pulled the grey archival box toward her and lifted out a diary so old its cover felt like dried leaves. Ms. Tanaka had set her up at a wide table near the window of the city archive, with cotton gloves and a foam cradle to rest the book in. "Settlers' diaries are primary sources," Ms. Tanaka had said. "They were written by the people who were actually there. Your job is to figure out what this one can tell you." Isla's assignment was to explain why people moved west in the 1800s, and she wanted an answer better than "because they wanted land," which was what her rough draft said.

Nya leaned over from the next table, where she was cataloguing photographs. "Find anything good?" Isla turned the pages carefully. The handwriting cramped and slanted, as if the writer had been jolted the whole time. One entry described a wagon wheel shattering on a rock. Another mentioned the writer's brother, whose knee had swollen after a fall; the diary said the doctor in the party thought the cartilage was damaged and that he might limp for life. An ox had gone lame. They had contracted with a guide to take them through the mountains, the diary said, and the guide had broken the agreement and vanished with their money.

Then Isla noticed something odd. Every entry through the spring of 1869 complained about dust, distance, and months on the trail. The writer counted the weeks since leaving Missouri and the number of graves passed. And then the entries simply stopped. There was one last page, dated 12 May 1869, and it was short and almost cheerful. We reached the town yesterday, it said. Uncle writes that the railroad was completed on 10 May 1869 at Promontory Summit, Utah. No more wagons for us. My cousin made the same trip west in days, not months, on the new train.

Isla sat back. Wait, she thought. The whole family had struggled along the trail for months, and then, right there near the end, the transcontinental railroad got finished and changed everything. Was that a coincidence, or was the diary sitting on a hinge in history? She looked at the map Ms. Tanaka had given her. The trail crossed a river at one point in a line almost perpendicular to their route, and the new railroad line curved across the map like a scar. People could still want land, she thought, but how badly they wanted it might depend on how hard it was to get there. Maybe the railroad didn't give people the wish to move. Maybe it removed the wall in front of a wish that was already there.

"Ms. Tanaka," she called softly, "can a diary just stop like that?" Ms. Tanaka came over, read the last page, and smiled. "Sometimes it stops because the writer's life changed. Check the inside back cover." Isla turned the cover. Pasted there was a folded scrap, a child's copy of a newspaper clipping about the celebration at Promontory Summit, with a hand-drawn locomotive at the top.

Nya abandoned her photographs entirely and pulled her chair over. "So what's your answer going to be?" Isla pulled her notebook close and began to write. "That people wanted to go west for lots of reasons," she said, "but for this family, before the railroad it cost them months and a brother's knee. Afterward it cost days. Same land, same dream, different wall." She underlined the date, 10 May 1869, twice, and added a small drawing of the little locomotive from the clipping.

activity: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
knowledge_domain: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
fact: Repeating an experiment several times helps show whether a result is real or just happened by chance.
story:
The ramp leaned against the porch steps exactly where Jacob had left it, a long board propped on the third stair, and across the kitchen table his notebook lay open to a page that said, in big letters, RACE RESULTS: RED CAR 1, BLUE CAR 0.

"Want to race again?" Nora asked, already kneeling at the top of the ramp. She had brought the blue car herself, a scratched thing with a wobbly wheel, and ever since Saturday she had been trying to win it back its honor. Saturday, the red car had beaten it by a full hand-span, and Jacob had crowed about it for the rest of the afternoon. "Best two out of three," she said.

"That's not fair," Jacob said. "The first race already proved red is faster." But he said it slowly, because something was nagging at him. He remembered a week ago, when he had guessed that the pantry mice came in through the gap under the back door. His dad had called it a hypothesis, a guess you could test, and when Jacob had stuffed the gap with steel wool and the droppings stopped appearing, the guess had held up. Guesses could hold up. He was starting to wonder if guesses could fall down, too.

"Then racing again shouldn't scare you," Nora said, and her whole face was eager, leaning forward on her knees. She wanted this win more than she wanted the last slice of pizza, and Jacob could see it.

"Fine. Go."

They released both cars together. The blue one shot down the board, its wobbly wheel humming, and crossed the flowerpot finish line a thumb-width ahead. Nora screamed. Jacob stared at the ramp as if it might magnify the moment into something he could study, some clue hiding in the wood.

They raced again. Blue won again, by even more. On the fifth race, red finally took one, wobbling past at the end like a tired runner.

Jacob sat back on his heels, doing the logic in his head. One race said red was faster. Five races said blue won three to two, and most of those by a lot. If he had stopped after Saturday, he would have believed the wrong thing forever, just because red happened to win once.

"So one race doesn't really prove anything," he said, mostly to himself. "It could just have happened by chance. You have to run it a bunch of times to see what's real."

Nora pumped the blue car over her head. "Then let's make it ten races," she said. "Right now. Loser sweeps the porch."

The board was still warm from the sun when Jacob set the cars side by side at the top. "Ready," he said, and let go.

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: Avoiding everything that causes anxiety brings quick relief but often makes the anxiety stronger over time, because the person never learns the situation is manageable.
story:
The notification buzzed at 9:14 on Sunday night. "BIO PRESENTATIONS TUESDAY," Elyas had written in the group chat, followed by three skull emojis. "Order is alphabetical so G gets to go third." Gabriella stared at her phone, then typed back, "I'll probably be absent again," and put the phone face down on her bed.

She had skipped the last one too. The teacher had let her hand in a written report instead, and for a whole day she had felt light, almost floaty, like she'd gotten away with something. But the first presentation, back in October, she had actually done. She remembered standing at the front of the room with her poster about tide pools, her voice shaky but audible, and surviving it. The November one she'd skipped. The December one she'd skipped. Somehow the October one had felt less scary than the November one, and the November one less scary than the idea of Tuesday.

"That's backwards," she muttered. The skipped ones should feel easier by now, since she'd had more time away from them. Unless skipping wasn't rest. Unless each skip was teaching her brain something.

The phone buzzed again. Niam: "Gabriella you can't demolish the entire grading period by missing every presentation." Elyas: "What happened to your tide pool one? That was actually good." Niam: "Consensus of the group chat: you should just do it. Even badly."

Gabriella picked the phone back up. Her thumbs hovered. She typed, "Every time I skip, the next one feels worse than the last. Does that happen to anyone else?" Niam replied fast: "That's the anxiety doing that, I think. My cousin calls avoidance a trap. Quick relief, then it comes back bigger." Elyas sent: "So Tuesday could be the scariest one yet OR you break the pattern and the one after Tuesday is smaller." Gabriella read that twice. It was testable. One data point either way.

She remembered the exact moment in October when she'd thought she might faint, and then hadn't. She hadn't fainted, hadn't run, hadn't even cried. The room had not ended. She had sat down and Elyas had whispered "nice starfish facts" and the day had continued like a normal day.

"Okay," she typed. "I'm doing it. But I need one thing." Niam: "Name it." "Nobody asks me questions at the end. I need that boundary or I'll bail." Elyas: "Deal. We'll intercept questions. Niam can fake-cough through them."

Tuesday morning, Mr. Gill called third name, hers. Gabriella walked up with her phone as a timer and her notes on crabs, and her hands were cold and her first sentence came out too fast. She made herself slow down on the second sentence. Nobody asked a question at the end. She sat down, and Niam slid a folded note across the desk that said "That was smaller than the tide pool one, right?"

In the group chat that afternoon she typed: "Data point collected. Next one in March. I already hate it, but less." Elyas replied, "Noted. Building a durable streak, one crab at a time." She set her phone down, then picked it up once more and added, "Remind me of this chat in March."

activity: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
knowledge_domain: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
fact: Rising action is the series of complications that raise the stakes and build tension before the climax.
story:
Ivy sat at the kitchen table with her notebook open to a page that said, at the top, THE DRAGON AND THE LOCKED GATE. Below the title there were three sentences, and the third one was the dragon arriving. She read the page aloud to herself, then frowned and read it again.

Marek came over after dinner, because he was writing a story for the same assignment and wanted to trade drafts. He read Ivy's page, chewing the strap of his backpack. "The dragon shows up and the gate melts in, like, two seconds," he said. "Then it's over. My whole story is like that too. Mr. Ferreira kept writing 'flat' on mine in red pen."

"Flat," Ivy repeated. She turned her pencil sideways and tapped it against her chin. "But the dragon is the biggest thing in my story. Shouldn't the biggest thing make it exciting?"

"Let's test it," Marek said. He pulled out his own draft, about a kid lost in a mall, and read it aloud, doing a squeaky voice to mimic the kid. The lost part happened in the first paragraph, and after that there was nothing left to wonder about. Ivy noticed that while he read, she stopped leaning forward. There was nothing to lean forward for.

She flipped back to her own notebook. "Okay, what if the dragon doesn't arrive right away? What if first the gate gets hot, then the guard dog growls at something nobody can see, then the key goes missing from its hook?" As she wrote each complication, the stakes felt like they were climbing stairs. She put quotation marks around everything the guard said, and a comma inside them before he said who was talking, the way Mr. Ferreira had circled on the board. "The part that raises the tension before the climax," she said slowly, "there must be a name for that. Rising action. That's probably the name."

They read her new draft out loud together, trading paragraphs. When the dragon finally melted the gate at the end, Marek actually sat up. "See, that's it. You made me wait for it."

At school the next morning, Ivy slid her story across the aisle before class started. Mr. Ferreira read it during silent reading time, and when he handed it back there was one word in the margin instead of red ink everywhere. "Durable," the note said, and under it, a small check mark. Ivy ran her thumb over the word, closed the notebook, and started planning the next one, with a locked lighthouse and a storm that came in three stages.

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: The law of supply says that when the price of a good rises, sellers usually offer more of it, because making and selling it becomes more profitable.
story:
The line outside the theater stretched past the bakery and around the corner, and Noemie counted heads while her friend Beckham counted minutes until the box office opened. Aditya had saved their spots at dawn, which felt like a serious obligation after he had given up his Saturday morning, so Noemie had brought him the last cinnamon bun from the bakery as payment. Only two hundred tickets were being sold at the window, and the line held at least three hundred people. That was the part Noemie kept turning over in her mind. Two hundred tickets, three hundred hands wanting them, one price. Why would the theater restrict the number sold when so many people were desperate to buy?

When the window opened, a loudspeaker announcement killed the mood. Face price was forty dollars, but a limited release meant the online price had jumped to ninety-five overnight, and the window tickets were nearly gone within the hour. Behind them, a man in a green jacket whispered that he had four extra tickets, ninety each, cash only. Noemie turned and saw something odd: another man two spots back was also selling extras, and a woman near the bakery had her phone out, listing tickets at ninety-two. Yesterday, one scalper in a line was normal. Today there were five, then seven.

"Where did all these sellers come from?" Noemie asked. "They were hiding under the bakery?"

Aditya shrugged. "Probably waiting. When the price was forty, selling an extra wasn't worth standing in line for hours. Now, at ninety-five, it is."

Noemie chewed on that. The price rose, and sellers appeared, more of them every ten minutes, each waving a phone or an envelope of tickets. She tested the idea the only way she could: she walked the line with a notepad, counting anyone openly offering tickets. First pass, seven. Second pass, twenty minutes later, eleven. The higher the posted online price climbed, the longer her list grew.

"That's the law of supply," Beckham said, peering over her notepad. "Price goes up, sellers offer more."

When Noemie and Aditya finally reached the window, the last tickets were gone, and the man in the green jacket raised his price to a hundred and ten as she watched. She looked down her notepad at the growing column of numbers, then back at the crowd of sellers still arriving from the parking lot.

"I wonder what happens tomorrow," she said, "when there are a hundred sellers and nobody left to buy."

activity: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
knowledge_domain: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
fact: In a 2007 study, people kept awake for a whole night showed about 60 percent stronger reactions to upsetting pictures in the amygdala, a brain area that responds to threats.
story:
Cole had stayed up all night gluing three hundred cotton balls onto a poster about democracy for Mr. Russo's class, and by morning the poster was beautiful and Cole felt like a cracked phone screen. He did not think much of it until Savanna leaned over at lunch and whispered, "Nice poster, cotton sheep," because a few of the cotton balls had wandered off the map of Greece. Cole stood up so fast his tray clattered, and he said something loud about her being a venomous little gossip. The whole cafeteria went quiet. Savanna blinked at him, stunned, and Cole sat back down with his ears burning.

That afternoon his mom scheduled him an appointment with Dr. Patel, whose office smelled like hand sanitizer and old magazines. The blood pressure cuff squeaked as it tightened around Cole's arm. "Sleeping okay?" she asked, and he had to confess that he had been awake since the night before, and before that he had been averaging maybe five hours a night for two weeks. She nodded like this was a math problem she had already solved.

"There was a study in 2007," she said, typing on her computer. "People kept awake for a whole night showed about sixty percent stronger reactions to upsetting pictures in the amygdala." She turned the screen so he could see a scan with a bright orange blob. "That's the amygdala. It's a brain area that responds to threats."

"Sixty percent," Cole repeated. "So my brain thought Savanna's joke was a threat because I'm tired."

"Your brain turned the volume knob up. The joke didn't get louder. Your hearing did." She showed him a breathing exercise: in for four counts, hold for four, out for six, three times. His shoulders, which had been riding up near his ears all day, dropped an inch. Then she wrote a routine on a prescription pad without medicine on it: screens off at ten, homework started at eight instead of eleven, same time every night, even weekends.

In the waiting room, Mr. Russo was sitting in the corner chair with a wrapped ankle, waiting for his own appointment, and he waved Cole over. "I heard about the cafeteria," he said. Cole explained the amygdala thing, the sixty percent, the upsetting pictures. Mr. Russo listened, then said, "So if I move the democracy project deadline earlier, my students will actually sleep and stop throwing trays. That's the best education research I've heard all year." He laughed at his own joke, which made it funnier somehow.

Cole decided to run an experiment on himself, the way the study people must have. On nights he followed the routine, he counted what set him off the next day: one annoying thing, maybe two, handled with breathing. The one night he stayed up until two finishing a level, Savanna hid his calculator as a prank and he felt his whole body go hot and tight, the volume knob cranked way up. He did four-four-six breathing right there at his desk, and by the third round the hot feeling had shrunk to something he could look at instead of something that owned him.

On Friday he caught Savanna at her locker. "I'm sorry I called you venomous," he said. "You're not. You're more like a bee. Technically annoying, but basically helpful."

Savanna squinted at him. "Was that an apology or an insult?"

"Sixty percent apology," Cole said, and she laughed so hard she had to lean on the locker.

activity: going on a school field trip with the class
knowledge_domain: going on a school field trip with the class
fact: In a fire, smoke and heat rise, so the cleaner, cooler air is near the floor, which is why firefighters teach people to crawl low under smoke.
story:
The bus smelled like grape juice and somebody's leftover sandwich, and Grace had spent the whole ride arguing with Eddy about what would be best at the science center. "The Van de Graaff generator," Eddy insisted. "Hair standing straight up. Obviously." Grace thought the fire safety wing sounded better, mostly because the permission slip had mentioned a smoke machine, and she wanted to know if the smoke was real or just fog from a machine like the one at the fall dance.

Ms. Grewal counted heads twice at the door, lost count once because Louka kept ducking behind the planetarium sign, and finally herded them toward the fire safety wing. "The gift shop revenue pays for half the exhibits here," she told them, "so buy a pencil if you want to keep the place running." Grace filed that away as a reason to buy two.

The wing had a practice room with padded walls and a doorway that belched billows of white haze from a machine in the corner. A firefighter in a station uniform stood by the door, but he mostly just said "stay low" and pointed. The haze hung in a thick layer near the ceiling, drifting and curling, and Grace noticed something odd: it wasn't sinking. It climbed. Wisps curled up along the walls like they were trying to touch the sprinklers.

Eddy walked straight into the cloud at full height, waving his arms like a windmill. "It's warm up here," he announced, coughing dramatically. Grace got down on her knees, mostly to laugh at him more comfortably, and realized the air near the floor was clear and cool. She put one hand high, where Eddy's head had been, and one hand low. The difference was like opening an oven versus opening a window. "The smoke and the heat go up," she said slowly, mostly to herself. "So the cleaner, cooler air is down here. That's why he keeps saying crawl."

She decided to test it. "Eddy, race you to the far door. You walk, I crawl." "That implies I'm going to lose," said Eddy. "It doesn't imply anything, it guarantees it," said Louka from behind them, already betting a fruit roll-up on Grace. Eddy strode into the haze, blind and coughing, while Grace crawled underneath the white layer, where she could see the whole room, the exit sign, and even the firefighter's boots. She reached the door a full ten seconds ahead.

"You're biased toward crawling forever now," Eddy said, handing Louka the fruit roll-up. "Maybe biased toward breathing," Grace said. The firefighter crouched down next to her and said, "Low and fast, that's the whole trick." Grace crawled one more lap just because she could, Louka timing her, the exit sign glowing above the smoke.

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: Coping means the ways a person handles stress or difficult feelings; healthy coping strategies include exercise, getting enough sleep and talking with someone trusted.
story:
Theo's hands were sweating before the nurse even called his name. He was at the doctor's office for a checkup, but the real problem was the vaccination scheduled at the end of it, and he had exactly forty minutes before the office closed at five o'clock. If he panicked and ran, there would be no second try today, and his mother would have to drag him back next week.

The waiting room smelled like antiseptic and old magazines. Theo sat between his mom and a boy from his class, Bentley, who was tapping his sneaker against the chair leg like a drumbeat. Bentley had a bad day written all over his face.

"Mrs. Riley moved the math test to tomorrow," Bentley muttered. "I got a fifty on the practice one." He crumpled a tissue in his fist. "My anxiety is through the roof."

Theo knew that word from the poster in Ms. Fraser's classroom. What he didn't know was what Bentley actually did about it. "What do you do after a day like that?"

"Xbox till midnight," Bentley said. "Then I feel like a zombie at school. It's ironic, I guess. I'm trying to feel better and I end up worse."

Theo thought about his own bad day last week, the one with the failed science quiz. He had ridden his bike around the block six times, gone to bed early, and told his dad the whole story at dinner. By morning the bad feeling had shrunk to the size of a pebble. He couldn't see why it had shrunk, exactly, which bugged him. Maybe it wasn't luck. Maybe it was a pattern he could test.

"Tomorrow, instead of the Xbox thing, try this," Theo said. "Ride your bike or shoot hoops, get to bed early, and tell somebody you trust about the test. My dad says that's coping, the ways you handle stress. Exercise, sleep, and talking to someone. It worked for me, I think."

"That's three things," Bentley said. "In one evening?"

"Two, if you talk while you shoot hoops."

The nurse called Theo's name, and his stomach flipped. He decided to run his own experiment right there. He squeezed the armrest, took five slow breaths, and said out loud, "I'm stressed about this needle, and I'm telling you because you're my friend."

Bentley laughed. "That was weirdly helpful."

The exam room was cold, and the paper on the table crunched when Theo climbed up. Ms. Fraser had once told the class that a good mentor doesn't fix things for you, they help you fix them yourself, and Theo decided he could be that for himself. When the doctor came in with the syringe, Theo looked at Bentley, who had talked his way into the room as moral support.

"Talk to me," Theo said. "Fast."

"So tomorrow, hoops at four, bed by nine," Bentley began, counting on his fingers. "And I'll tell my brother about the fifty before I bury myself in Xbox."

The needle went in. Theo barely felt it.

activity: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
knowledge_domain: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
fact: In belly breathing, also called diaphragmatic breathing, the belly rises as you breathe in instead of the shoulders lifting, which lets the lungs fill more deeply.
story:
The night hike sign-up sheet hung on the mess hall door all week, and Wyatt had put his name on it the first morning, before he knew that the trail ended at a ledge above Miller's Gorge. Now it was Tuesday, and Thursday was coming fast. He could not stop imagining the drop, which was absurd, because he had never even seen the gorge, only heard Archer talk about it in a voice that made it sound like the edge of the world.

That night in the cabin, Wyatt lay awake counting the knots in the pine boards above his bunk. His shoulders felt tight, and his breathing came quick and shallow, like he was jogging while lying still. Across the room Archer was already asleep, and Andreanne's flashlight glowed faintly through the curtain that divided the girls' side. The counselor had said something at dinner about nerves, something Wyatt hadn't listened to properly, except for two words: breathing, and belly.

In the morning he found Andreanne by the canoe rack. "When you're stressed, where does your breathing go?" he asked. She put a hand flat on her stomach and a hand on her shoulder and breathed in. Her belly rose. Her shoulder didn't move at all. Wyatt tried it the way he'd been doing all night, and the opposite happened: his shoulders lifted and his belly stayed flat. "That's why mine doesn't work," he said. "I've been doing it backwards."

"The counsellor called it diaphragmatic breathing," Andreanne said. "The belly rises when you breathe in, instead of the shoulders lifting. That way your lungs fill more deeply." She breathed in again to show him, slow, her hand rising like a small tide. Wyatt copied her. In through the nose, belly up. Out, belly down. After ten tries his shoulders had loosened without his telling them to.

That afternoon Mr. Shin, the camp director, stopped him on the path. "You look tired, Wyatt. Skipping sleep?" Wyatt admitted he'd lain awake for two nights. Mr. Shin suggested a routine: same bedtime each night, no flashlight comics under the blanket, a few slow breaths before the lamp went out. "Routine can insulate you from a racing mind," he said, "like a jacket against cold."

Thursday evening, the group hiked out through a stretch where a burn years ago had left the slope barren and grey, nothing but stone and stubble. At the top, the sun dropped low and an orange haze settled over the gorge, a phenomenon the counsellor called valley light. Wyatt stood at the ledge, put a hand on his belly, and breathed in slowly. His hand rose. His shoulders stayed still. Archer tapped him on the shoulder and pointed down at the river far below. "Check that out," Archer said.

activity: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
knowledge_domain: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
fact: Some linear equations are true for every number, such as 2x + 2 = 2(x + 1), because both sides are the same expression written differently.
story:
Vincent stayed after the bell on Thursday because his quiz on equations had come back with a 61 circled in red, and his father had said no ski trip until it was a B. Ms. Pierre's tutoring session met in Room 12, where the desks had been pushed into a circle and the whiteboard still showed lunch menus from the cafeteria monitor group. Vincent sat with his notebook open and his pencil doing nothing, because the problem in front of him refused to move.

Solve for x, the worksheet said. 2x + 2 = 2(x + 1). He knew the rule now, mostly: whatever you do to one side, you do to the other. He'd learned it the hard way three weeks ago, when he'd subtracted from only the left side and Ms. Pierre had made him check his answer by plugging it back in. It hadn't fit. The rule felt like carrying a box with two people, each side needing the same lift or the whole thing tips.

Kristen was at the board, because she'd raised her hand fastest, which annoyed Jake so much he'd knocked his eraser off the desk on purpose. She distributed the 2 on the right side carefully, writing 2x + 2 = 2x + 2. Then she subtracted 2x from both sides. The room went quiet except for the radiator. What remained on the board was 2 = 2.

"That's wrong," Jake said immediately. "You lost the x. You can't solve something with no letter in it." Kristen stood there with the marker against her chin, and Ms. Pierre, who usually jumped in with questions, only folded her arms and waited, which Vincent had learned meant something interesting was happening. Kristen wrote nothing. The marker stayed where it was.

Vincent stared at the 2 = 2. If the x was gone, then no number could break the equation, because there was nothing left to break. He decided to test it, quiet and low, in the margin of his notebook. Try x = 5. Left side: 10 plus 2, which was 12. Right side: 5 plus 1 was 6, doubled, also 12. He tried x = 100. Both sides gave 202. His pulse did a strange little jump, the kind he got when a puzzle box clicked open. From the numbers he could infer that any number he picked would land on a match, though he wanted one more to be sure. x = 0. Both sides gave 2. The pattern was stable; it never wobbled.

"Check a number," he called out before he could talk himself out of it. Kristen glanced over, then tried x = 5 on the board, working both sides down to 12. She tried x = 100. Her eyes went wide.

"It doesn't matter what x is," she said slowly. "It's true for every number."

Ms. Pierre smiled and wrote the word identity at the top of the board, and Vincent copied it down, then copied it again in his neatest handwriting, because something told him it was going to be on the retake.

"Okay," Jake said, standing up. "My turn. Give me one with an actual answer in it."

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: In the United States, the cost of crude oil is usually the largest single part of the price of a gallon of gasoline, so pump prices tend to rise when crude oil prices rise.
story:
The last four jars of tropical mango salsa sat on the top shelf, and Theo needed three of them for the seventh-grade fundraiser on Friday. The class had voted, the budget was set, and Ms. Rowe had signed the permission slip. But when he turned the jar over, the price tag read $6.49, and he distinctly remembered it being $4.99 two weeks ago, because he had checked twice before asking his dad for the money.

"You're kidding," said Patience, appearing beside him with her own basket. She was saving her allowance to buy the salsa too, for her brother's birthday, because he'd tried it at a restaurant once and talked about it for a month. "Six forty-nine? That's all my money and then some."

"There were tons of jars here before spring break," Theo said. "The whole shelf was full." He looked at the empty space around the four remaining jars, then at the little orange sign the store had slipped under the tag. It said LIMITED QUANTITY in small letters, as if apologizing.

His dad was waiting outside at the gas pump, and through the window Theo could see the numbers on the pump screen climbing higher than usual. A kid about his age, waiting in the next car with his mom, leaned out and asked his mom why the price had gone up since last week. "Crude oil," his mom said, checking her phone. "The cost of crude oil is usually the biggest single part of the price of a gallon of gas, so when crude goes up, the pump price goes up too." Theo filed that away without knowing why, the way you pocket a coin you find on the sidewalk.

Inside, he stood in the aisle and worked it out out loud. "So the salsa got popular. Everybody wants it, and there's hardly any left, so the store charges more. If people will pay it, why not?" Patience frowned at a jar like it had personally offended her. "Then if they make a bunch more, and nobody's fighting over it, the price should come back down." Theo decided to test it. He would monitor the shelf every time they came for groceries this month, writing the price and the number of jars in his notebook, the same notebook where he tracked the fundraiser's revenue, which so far was eleven dollars and a promise from Ryleigh.

That Friday they sold the salsa at the fundraiser anyway, at cost, because Ms. Rowe chipped in the difference. Two weeks later Theo came back and found the shelf packed solid with jars, rows and rows of them, the orange sign gone. The tag read $4.99. He wrote it down, showed the page to Patience, and she went to get a cart.

"Two jars," she said. "Birthday present. And I'm grabbing one for you, because you called it."

activity: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
knowledge_domain: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
fact: Teasing often depends on an audience, so walking away with the targeted classmate, saying something like "Come on, let's go," can end it without a confrontation.
story:
The party at Grandpa's house had spilled onto the porch, and Louis was balancing a plate of samosas when he heard the laughing. Three boys from the neighborhood had cornered Eleonore by the porch rail. One of them held up her sketchbook, flipping through the pages while she reached for it, her face going red.

"Nice rat," the tallest boy said, tapping a drawing. "You spend all weekend drawing one little rodent?"

Louis's first instinct was to yell at them, to say something loud that would oppose them in front of everybody. He'd tried that once at school last fall, when kids were teasing Elissa about her accent. He'd shouted, the teasers had shouted back, and somehow Elissa had ended up crying while he got a lecture from Ms. Cruz about escalating conflicts. The teasing hadn't stopped for weeks. He still remembered standing in the hallway feeling like he'd made everything worse.

He set down his plate and thought about it instead. What had actually fed the teasing that day? It wasn't just the mean words. It was the ring of kids watching, grinning, waiting to see what happened next. The boys with the sketchbook kept glancing around at their audience, playing bigger because people were looking.

So Louis tried a different idea. He walked over, not to the boys but to Eleonore, and put a hand on her shoulder.

"Come on, let's go," he said. "Grandpa needs help with the snacks in the kitchen."

Eleonore blinked at him, then seemed to catch on. "Right. The snacks," she said.

They walked toward the door together. Behind them, the tallest boy called out something about the rat drawing again, but his voice landed on nothing. No audience, no laughter, no game. When Louis glanced back, the boys were already drifting toward the yard, the sketchbook abandoned on the rail. Eleonore doubled back and picked it up.

In the kitchen, Grandpa had them arrange biscuits on a tray, which was a trivial job that took two minutes, but they stretched it out because it was quiet in there. "Thanks," Eleonore said, smoothing a bent page. "They've been doing that since I moved here. I figured if I ignored them they'd quit, but they never did."

"Last time I tried to fight people off, it got worse," Louis said. "I yelled at some kids picking on my friend Elissa. Everybody just gathered around to watch."

Eleonore considered this, arranging a biscuit. "So they need a crowd."

"Seems like it," Louis said. "Take away the crowd, and there's nothing to perform for."

Later, when they carried the tray back out, the boys had moved on to a soccer game in the yard. One of them mumbled something about the drawing as they passed, but he was already running after the ball, and nobody laughed.

A week later at school, Louis saw it again: a knot of kids near the lockers, laughing at Elissa's boots, which were two different colors on purpose. He didn't raise his voice. He just walked up beside her and said, "Come on, we'll be late for science." They walked off together, and behind them the knot loosened and broke apart, kids wandering off to class with nothing left to watch.

At lunch, Elissa slid her tray next to his. "Where'd you learn that trick?"

"Grandpa's porch," Louis said. "Eleonore drew a hamster."

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: Gleaning is an ancient practice: the Book of Leviticus in the Hebrew Bible tells farmers to leave the edges of their fields unharvested for the poor and for strangers.
story:
Nathan stood at the long steel counter of the soup kitchen, pressing his palms into a mountain of raw carrots. Orange dust clung to his fingers, and the air smelled of onions and bleach. His job, Mr. Leblanc had said, was to chop. He wanted to earn his service hours, but mostly he wanted to be useful, and so far he had only managed to slice his thumb.

"Rocks," said Jaxen beside him, who had the easier job of sorting bread. "Some of these carrots are basically rocks."

"Then persevere," Nathan said, quoting his gym teacher, and he kept chopping even though his arm burned and his stamina was gone by the second bin. Behind them, the lunch line was already forming, and through the serving window he could hear trays clatter and a woman asking for extra rice for later.

That was when Nathan noticed something odd. The vegetable bins were almost empty, but back by the loading door, a stack of crates sat untouched. Every few minutes a gray-haired volunteer walked over, pulled a few bruised apples and crooked carrots from the crates, and set them in a small basket marked "Ed's rack." Nathan watched three more times before he was sure. Whatever rule governed that rack, it wasn't written anywhere, and Mr. Leblanc was too busy to ask.

He tested it anyway. While carrying scraps to the compost, he paused by the crates and lifted out a dented but perfect pear. He set it on Ed's rack. The old volunteer, small and bent with what he claimed was hereditary back trouble, glanced over and nodded once, so Nathan started moving everything slightly imperfect, the bruised, the crooked, the small, onto the rack too.

"You glean," the old man said, surprising him. "My grandfather called it that. Gleaning. In the Book of Leviticus, in the Hebrew Bible, farmers are told to leave the edges of their fields unharvested, for the poor and for strangers."

"So the ugly food is the edge of the field," Nathan said slowly, and the old man laughed and pointed at the door, where a family with two grocery bags and no trays was coming in early, before the line formed. They went straight to the rack. A boy about seven grabbed the dented pear like it was treasure.

The twist landed at cleanup time. Mr. Leblanc inspected Nathan's station and frowned at the empty crates, all the imperfect produce gone. "Who emptied those? That's tomorrow's compost demo." Nathan's stomach dropped, until the old volunteer shuffled over and set the last bruised apple on the counter between them.

"That demo," the old man said, "can use a nice apple instead."

Mr. Leblanc looked at the apple, then at the empty rack by the door, then at Nathan's bandaged thumb. "Fine. But you're on carrot duty again next Saturday, so build up that stamina." Jaxen slid the last loaf of bread into the basket marked "Ed's rack" without a word, and the seven-year-old outside the window waved with his pear juice still on his chin.

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: When a phone takes a photo with location services on, it can write the exact GPS coordinates of where the photo was taken into hidden data in the file, called EXIF metadata.
story:
Nathan set his phone face-down beside his plate, then turned it over again, because the whole reason he'd brought it to the table was the photo. Curtis had sent it at recess: a picture of his new bike leaning against his garage, with the caption "guess what I got." Nathan had opened the photo's file information just now, out of curiosity, and under a heading he'd never noticed before there was a map. A little red pin sat on the map. When he tapped it, it zoomed in to a street with a symmetrical row of houses, and one of them was Curtis's, because Nathan recognized the blue recycling bin shaped like a rocket ship. His dad looked up from his pasta. "You're allowed the phone at dinner if you're solving a mystery," his dad said. "You look like you're solving a mystery."

"The photo knows where Curtis lives," Nathan said. "Not just because the garage is in it. I mean it knows. There's a map inside the picture file." His little sister stopped chewing long enough to say that was impossible, and Nathan admitted it sounded impossible, which was exactly why he wanted to check. He explained, carefully, that when a phone takes a photo with location services on, it can write the exact GPS coordinates of where the photo was taken into hidden data in the file. "It's called EXIF metadata," he said, reading the heading off the screen. "That's the word. Metadata." His dad put down his fork. "Send me a photo from the kitchen," his dad said. "Right now, before your soup gets cold."

That was the test. Nathan took a picture of the salt shaker, sent it to his dad's phone, and his dad opened the file information and tapped the little map. A red pin appeared, and it sat squarely on their own house, on their own street, as if the salt shaker had a home address. His sister leaned across the table so far that her elbow obstructed Nathan's view of the screen, and she went quiet in a way she almost never did. "It's like the photo keeps a receipt," his dad said. "Except the receipt says where you were standing."

Nathan thought about the recess photos kids sent all day long, and how a stranger who got one could tap the same thing he'd tapped. He wasn't sure strangers could get them, but he wasn't sure they couldn't, either. "Curtis posts everything," he said. "He posted from the dentist last week when he was getting his antibiotic for his tooth, and his location thing was on then too, I bet." He picked up his phone and started typing, then stopped and deleted it, because a text that said "your photos know your address" would just sound weird.

He tried again. "Ask your dad to look at the map in the info thing," he typed to Curtis. "Do it before you post the bike one." Under the table, his foot bounced while he waited. The reply came before his mom finished serving the salad. "HOW DID YOU GET A MAP OF MY HOUSE," Curtis wrote, in all capitals. Nathan held the screen up so his dad could see it. "Tell him to come over after dinner," his dad said. "We'll turn it off together."

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: Akira Kurosawa's 1950 film Rashomon tells one crime through four witnesses whose accounts contradict each other.
story:
The classroom door was open when it should have been locked, the marker tray was on the floor, and the class mouse, Biscuit, was missing from her tank. Ms. Lombardi stood in the doorway with her coffee and said, "Nobody leaves until we figure this out." Biscuit was a small brown rodent with a talent for squeezing through gaps, but she had never escaped before, and the tank lid was not just open, it was on the other side of the room.

Ms. Lombardi interviewed the four students who had been in after school for film club. Cassidy went first. "I left at three fifteen. The lid was on the tank then, and the door was shut." Jaida said the lid was already off when she got her backpack, and that she had definitely closed the door behind her. A boy from another class said he saw a teacher come in around four, and the fourth student, quiet all year, said he heard something fall but didn't look up from his book. Every account contradicted the others, and by lunch nobody trusted anybody, which was a lot of drama for one escaped mouse.

Scarlett wrote all four versions on the whiteboard while the others argued. She began to hypothesize that the witnesses weren't lying, that each one had seen a real piece of the event and had filled in the rest. If that was true, the pieces should fit together like a puzzle instead of cancelling each other out. She looked at the board. Lid on at three fifteen. Lid off by three forty. A noise after four. Door open at five. She tested it by crawling along the bookshelf, the only path a mouse could take from the tank to the far corner.

Behind the dictionaries she found Biscuit, curled in a nest of shredded paper, and next to the nest, a blue pen. The fourth student's pen, the one he had said he lost days ago. That meant he had been near the shelf, which meant he had taken the lid off, though probably to show Biscuit to his little brother and not to free her into a life of dictionary nests. When Scarlett carried the mouse back in her cupped hands, the whole class stopped arguing at once, which was almost disappointing.

"That's like Rashomon," Cassidy said, staring at the whiteboard. "Akira Kurosawa's 1950 film. One crime, four witnesses, and all four stories contradict each other."

"Except nobody here committed a crime," said Ms. Lombardi. "Just a mouse with a plan."

The quiet student admitted the lid, apologized to Biscuit rather than to anyone else, and volunteered to be the diligent one who checked the latch every afternoon. Jaida taped a sign to the tank that said NOT A DOOR. Scarlett erased the board slowly, keeping the last line visible until the end of the period: four stories, one mouse, and one blue pen that had been telling the truth the whole time.

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
fact: After flying across time zones, the body clock adjusts at an average of about one day for each hour of time difference.
story:
The ferry pulled away from the dock just after sunrise, and Arianna found a bench near the railing where she could watch the harbour shrink. Six days ago her family had flown across the ocean for this trip, six hours of time zones packed into a single plane ride, and her body still refused to accept the local clock. Last night, the second night, she had lain in the hotel bed wide awake at midnight, listening to the fridge hum, while her parents slept like stones.

Gwen from the hotel's kids' club came and sat beside her, holding a paper cup of hot chocolate. "I've been looking for you everywhere," Gwen said. "I want to see the whales from the front deck, but they only come up near the islands, and my dad says we'll be at the snack bar by then. He works for some corporation and he's on his phone the whole trip. He never notices anything."

Arianna looked at the grey water and thought about her sleepless nights. On the first night she had assumed it was the strange bed. On the second night, still awake at midnight, she had started counting on her fingers. Six hours of time difference, and the second night had felt almost no better than the first. She tried a rule in her head, one day for each hour, and it fit. Six hours meant six days, and they were only on day three. There were three more nights of this. It was not the bed, and it was not her imagination. It was arithmetic.

"That's not normal," Gwen said, watching her count. "What are you doing?"

"Working out a rule," Arianna said. "It's jet lag. Your body clock adjusts at about one day for each hour of time difference. We flew six hours, so it'll take about six days." As soon as she said it out loud, she tested it against her aunt, who had flown the same route and had complained of waking at dawn for nearly a week. It fit her too.

Gwen's eyes went wide. "Six days? Then we're both off schedule at the same time." She stood up. "Come on. If you're going to be awake at midnight anyway, that's when you can see the stars from the front deck. And tomorrow morning, before anyone's up, we'll take the conventional early ferry, the boring one nobody takes, and we'll have the islands all to ourselves. The whales come up at first light."

"Your dad won't come," Arianna said.

"He will if we get his ticket," Gwen said, "and if we promise to let him drink his coffee in silence." She held out her hand, and the hot chocolate wobbled in the other. "So, deal? Day six, everything goes back to normal. Until then, we own the night."

Arianna took her hand. Out past the rail, a gull dropped low over the water and scooped something silver up in its beak.

activity: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
knowledge_domain: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
fact: Brackets are cleared with the distributive property before solving: 3(x + 2) becomes 3x + 6, because the 3 multiplies both terms inside.
story:
The note had been waiting on Charlie's locker since third period, folded into a lopsided triangle. "Retest Thursday," it said, in Mr. Haile's blocky handwriting. "Solve 3(x + 2) = 18. Show every step." Below that he'd drawn a small smiling sun, which somehow made it worse.

Charlie walked to the corner store after school because that was where Dante worked the counter on Tuesdays, and Dante was the only person she knew who did equations for fun. The bell on the door chimed. Dante was restocking candy bars without hurrying, as if the weekend were imminent and nothing before it mattered.

"I got minus four," Charlie said, slapping her practice sheet on the counter. "Mr. Haile said check it, so I checked it, and it doesn't verify. Three times minus four is negative twelve, plus two is negative ten, and that is not eighteen."

Dante picked up the sheet. He read it the way the store's motion sensor read customers, slowly and without opinion. "Here's your trouble. You multiplied the three by the x only. See the brackets? The three outside has to hit both things inside. So 3(x + 2) turns into 3x + 6."

"That's it? It just... multiplies both?"

"That's the whole trick. It's called the distributive property." He slid the sheet back. "Brackets come down first, then you solve."

Charlie borrowed a pen from beside the register and wrote 3x + 6 = 18. Then she thought about the scales bolted to the counter for weighing candy, and how if you took six off one side you had to take six off the other or the needle lied. She subtracted six from both sides: 3x = 12. She divided both sides by three. x = 4. She checked it. Three times four was twelve, plus six was eighteen, and for the first time in a week the universe made sense. "It verifies," she said, with the dignity of a detective closing a case.

The door chimed again and Ludovic came in, jacket still on, holding his own crumpled retest notice. He looked at Charlie's sheet, then at her face, and clearly decided not to ask. "Slushie," he said to Dante. "Blue."

"On your money," Dante said, but he was already filling the cup, because that was how the store worked: rules stated firmly, then quietly bent.

Charlie copied her work onto a clean page for Ludovic, drawing the brackets with heavy little arches so he could not miss them. At the bottom she added a line for him to check his own answer, and next to it she wrote, in her best imitation of Mr. Haile's block capitals, "Show every step." Ludovic frowned at the paper, then at the candy scale, and Charlie watched him take his slushie to the back table and start counting terms on his fingers.

"Blue ones are two for a dollar today," Dante called after her as the door chimed. Charlie took two.

activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
knowledge_domain: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
fact: Like humans, guinea pigs cannot make their own vitamin C, so they must get it from their food every day.
story:
Rosalie carried the cardboard box into the kitchen and set it on the table. Inside, the guinea pig, a brown and white one she had named Button, sat in the corner nibbling a pellet. Her mother had signed the adoption papers that morning, and the drive home had preceded Rosalie's first real job: figuring out what a guinea pig actually needed.

For three days Button ate dry pellets and hay, and Rosalie refilled the water bottle each morning. On the fourth day Button stayed in her hideout and did not come out for food. Rosalie lifted the hideout and saw that Button's eyes were half shut and she had not touched the pellets from the night before.

Rosalie called Emmie, who had two rabbits. "She won't eat," Rosalie said. "The pellets are the same as always."

"Rabbits get sick like that too," Emmie said. "Did you change anything?"

"That's the thing. Nothing changed. That's the whole concept, it's exactly the same every day." Rosalie hung up and sat on the kitchen floor with her phone, searching. She found a page about guinea pigs and stopped at one line. Like humans, guinea pigs cannot make their own vitamin C, so they must get it from their food every day.

She read it twice. Pellets came from a bag, dry and old, and she had given nothing fresh, not once. If Button could not make vitamin C herself, then days of pellets and hay might mean days of none. She did not know that was the cause, but it was probable, and it was the one thing she could test.

Rosalie went to the refrigerator and pulled out a bell pepper. She cut a strip, rinsed it, and set it in the cage. Then she waited without moving. Button came out slowly, sniffed the strip, and took a bite. Then another. Rosalie let out a breath and texted Kenzie: she's eating. it was the vitamin C. they can't make it themselves, it has to be in their food every single day.

"Every single day," she said out loud, and wrote it on a sticky note.

The next morning Button was at the front of the cage, standing up on her back legs, squeaking before Rosalie even opened the refrigerator door.

activity: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
knowledge_domain: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
fact: At the equinoxes, around March 20 and September 22, day and night are roughly equal in length all over Earth.
story:
Ryder had one job on this camping trip: figure out how to explain the seasons to his class on Monday, and he had promised Ms. Addo it would not involve the word "just." "Don't tell us it's just because Earth is tilted," she had said. "Show us why that matters." Now he sat by the tent with a flashlight, an orange, and a marker-drawn equator line, while Francisco poked the campfire and Alia video-called her cousin in Australia.

"Try it now," Alia said, holding up her phone. On the screen, her cousin waved from a porch in the late afternoon light. Ryder leaned in. "What time does the sun set there today?" he asked. "About the same as here, actually," the cousin said. "Weird, right?" Ryder frowned. He had assumed Australia, being on the far side of the world, would be a full day ahead or behind, but that wasn't the same as sunset times. He made Alia ask again to be sure. September 22, the cousin said, and the sun would drop below the horizon at almost exactly the hour it would back home. Twelve hours of day, twelve hours of night, on both sides of the planet.

"That's the equinox," Francisco said from the fire, without looking up. "My mom calls it that." He held up the stick he was roasting marshmallows on. "Means equal night, or something." Alia wrote it down. Ryder picked up the orange and turned it slowly, trying to picture where the day side and night side had to split so that both places got the same share.

He jammed the roasting stick straight through the orange, pole to pole, then tilted it. Francisco held the flashlight dead level, the "sun," and Ryder spun the fruit. The marker line showed half in light, half in shadow. But when he tilted the stick far over and spun it again, one hemisphere caught light well past its halfway line while the other sat mostly in the dark. "There," Ryder said. "That's a solstice, maybe. One half gets the long days." He tilted it back to straight up. Spin. Equal halves again. He tilted it just a little. Spin. Nearly equal, both halves.

"So the tilt isn't the whole story by itself," Alia said, watching the orange. "It's the tilt plus where we are in the orbit." Ryder nodded so hard he nearly dropped the fruit. "Because if it were distance from the sun, everything on Earth would have summer at the same time, and Australia wouldn't have winter when we have summer." Francisco pointed the flashlight at him. "And at the equinoxes, around March 20 and September 22, the day and night are roughly equal everywhere. Not just here. Everywhere."

The three of them argued about the marshmallows until the supply was gone. They made a treaty: Francisco would handle the flashlight during Monday's demonstration, Alia would hold the orange, and Ryder would do all the talking. The vote was unanimous, three to zero, with one abstention from Alia's cousin on the small screen, who claimed a marshmallow by video.

Ryder practiced once more in the tent's doorway, tilting the orange toward the flashlight while moths circled the lantern and the campfire's glow began to diminish behind the trees. "Watch the line," he said quietly, to nobody, to Monday, to the whole tilted spinning world. "Watch what happens to the line."

activity: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
knowledge_domain: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
fact: Shirley Jackson's story The Lottery, published in The New Yorker in 1948, opens with children piling up stones, a detail that hints at how the lottery ends.
story:
Norah curled into the window seat of her reading nook with her notebook, a striped blanket, and a photocopy of the story her class had finished that afternoon. Ms. Kaya had given them one task for tomorrow: find a detail in the first paragraph that hints at how the story ends, and be ready to explain what it suggests. The assignment was temporary, due in the morning, but it felt like a locked door. Norah had read the opening three times and all she could see was a sunny small-town morning, flowers blooming, grass richly green.

Her phone buzzed against the cushion. It was Marley, texting from down the street: "I picked the black box. That has to be it, right?" Norah typed back that she had guessed the same thing, then hesitated. The box showed up in the middle of the story, not the first paragraph, and Ms. Kaya had been specific. She pulled the blanket tighter, breathing in the dusty smell of old paper, and read the opening aloud one more time, slowly, the way you might run your fingers along a wall looking for a hidden seam.

Then she stopped. "Bobby Martin had already stuffed his pockets full of stones," she read, "and the other boys soon followed his example, selecting the smoothest and roundest stones." Children. Piling up stones. On a morning that had seemed so calm. Her reflex was to flip the page and check the ending again, and when she did, the connection hit her so hard that she sat up and knocked her mug of cocoa, which wobbled but survived. The stones were there at the end too. The first paragraph had been telling readers what was coming all along, hiding it in plain sight.

Marley rang the doorbell ten minutes later, still holding his own photocopy. "Okay, show me," he said, squeezing into the nook beside her, his elbow cold from the walk. Norah pointed at the sentence about Bobby Martin. "It's the stones," she said. "The story is Shirley Jackson's 'The Lottery,' and it came out in The New Yorker in 1948. She opens with kids collecting stones, and that's the hint about how the lottery ends." Marley stared at the page, mouth open, then smacked his forehead with the paperback.

"I wrote two paragraphs about the box," he groaned. Norah laughed and tore a fresh page from her notebook for him, because Ms. Kaya had said they could share ideas as long as each of them explained the thinking in his own words. They sat shoulder to shoulder, pencils scratching, while the sky outside the nook turned the color of a bruise. Somewhere in her mind, Norah knew she would cherish this feeling, the moment a hidden pattern gave itself up. Marley read his sentence out loud, then leaned over and tapped her page. "You wrote 'the grass was richly green' twice," he said. "Better cross one out before Ms. Kaya counts it."

activity: to improvise a blues solo over a twelve-bar chord progression
knowledge_domain: to improvise a blues solo over a twelve-bar chord progression
fact: Bending a guitar string pushes it sideways and stretches it tighter, which raises the note's pitch.
story:
